newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: S'pore Oct gas oil swaps traded at record $28.40.
newsitem.headline: S'pore Oct gas oil swaps traded at record $28.40.

text.p: Singapore gas oil swaps soared to trade at a record high on Monday, while physical cargo prices are poised to top its five-year record trade of $27.90 per barrel, industry sources said.
October gas oil swaps traded at $28.30, $28.35 and $28.40, above its previous record of $28.10 chalked up earlier this month following the U.S. missile attack on Iraqi defense sites, brokers said.
The October market was last quoted at $28.40/28.50, a big jump over the month's low of $26.80 traded on September 17, when India cancelled its November import tender.

At that time, crude fell sharply on reports that the U.S. had asked Saudi Arabia to raise its crude exports to compensate for the delay in Iraqi crude sales. November Brent plunged to $21.55 on the report, which was later denied by both parties. Brent is currently trading at $23.55.
Sources said the Singapore market is largely driven by factors in the west, such as low heating oil stocks in the U.S. and peak winter demand in Europe.
October gas oil futures on London's IPE traded earlier on Monday at a five-year high of $234.50 per tonne.
"The market is dragged up by western futures. The supply and demand balance does not warrant such strong prices," one refiner said.
Although prices were driven up by western factors, refiners in Asia have no difficulty selling their product at these prices, the refiner said.
Physical premiums in Singapore are steady at 40 cents per barrel to Singapore spot quotes and trades have been done recently at these levels, one trader said.
Sellers are not distressed as there are no arbitrage cargoes coming in to this region from the Middle East, traders said.
Middle East cargoes are currently exported to Africa and the Mediterranean where they fetch better prices, one trader said.
Last week Middle East cargoes were sold at around $1.00 per barrel premium to MidEast spot quotes and these cargoes were shipped to North Africa and East Africa, a trader said.

In Asia, players continue to look to China and Indonesia for outlets. China last week bought one spot cargo at $218 per tonne on a cost-and-freight basis and was said to be bidding last week around $215. China is closed for a three-day holiday which will put a pause on trading.
Indonesia is still looking to buy October gas oil to cover the shutdown of the 125,000-barrel-per-day Balongan refinery beginning October 1 for 24 days, a trader said.
